I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Conducted by CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, it is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey, collecting data since 1957 from about 27,000 adults each year through confidential, face-to-face interviews.

prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

National Health Interview Survey
 

About NHIS

For Everyone
June 18, 2026

What to know

  • NHIS is the National Health Interview Survey.
  • NHIS is a national survey that monitors the health of the U.S. population.
  • NHIS statistics provide insights into the health of people of different ages, sexes, races and ethnicities, geographic locations, and social and economic circumstances.

Overview

The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of people across the country—the U.S. population—by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics. NHIS focuses on the health of U.S. children and adults.

CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) conducts NHIS. It is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey. NHIS began collecting data in 1957.

Each year, NHIS collects data from about 27,000 adults through confidential, face-to-face interviews throughout the year. Many of these adults also provide health information about children in their households.

NHIS collects data from civilians who don't live in institutions. Civilians are people not serving on active duty in the military. Institutionalized people live in places like correctional facilities, skilled-nursing homes, and mental (psychiatric) hospitals.

NCHS is exploring new ways for you to participate in NHIS. Some people may receive a paper questionnaire while others will receive an invitation to complete the survey online. Some people may receive both. Your participation matters no matter how you complete the survey. If you need assistance with the survey or have questions, please call the number on the letter you received or email nhis@census.gov.

Selected to participate in the survey?

Learn why you should take part in NHIS and what to expect.
Visit our participant website

What's collected

NHIS collects data through personal interviews. One adult household member provides information about their own health and the health of others in their households.

NHIS collects data about health topics like—

  • Illness and chronic conditions
  • Injuries and chronic pain
  • Health-related behaviors
  • Ability to perform daily activities (functioning) and disability
  • Healthcare access and use
  • Health insurance coverage
  • Preventive services to identify and prevent health problems

The U.S. Census Bureau employs and trains field staff to conduct these interviews. They follow procedures developed by NCHS experts. Field staff conduct most interviews in person. Sometimes they conduct follow-up interviews over the phone.

Did you know?

NHIS content is updated about every 15–20 years to reflect advances in survey methodology and coverage of health topics. In 2019, NHIS launched redesigned content and structure that differs from the earlier questionnaire design (1997–2018).

Data and documentation

NCHS publishes reports featuring expert analysis of NHIS data. Selected estimates also are available as part of our interactive data query systems that provide tables and charts.

In producing these resources, NHIS staff prioritize protecting participants' privacy.

Data files

NHIS public use data files are available to download in multiple formats. All potentially identifiable information has been removed to ensure the confidentiality of participants and their households.

NHIS restricted data files are available through the National Center for Health Statistics Research Data Center (RDC) for a fee. To access restricted NHIS data, researchers must submit requests in the Standard Application Process portal. The RDC provides instructions for preparing and submitting an application to access restricted data.

NHIS data also has been linked with data from other sources. This provides more robust datasets that can be used to analyze complex relationships between data from different sources. These linked datasets are available in the RDC.

Find data documentation for these datasets at Questionnaires, Datasets, and Documentation.

How the data are used

NCHS staff use NHIS data to produce official national health estimates. One of NHIS's key strengths is its ability to produce estimates for many subgroups of the U.S. population. NHIS can do this because it collects data from such a large group of people.

NHIS health statistics provide health information by—

  • Demographic characteristics, like age and marital status
  • Geographic location, like region and metro area size
  • Social and economic circumstances, like employment status and poverty level

These data help researchers, policymakers, and other data users better understand how health differs among these groups.

NHIS data drive policies and programs to improve health. NHIS results have helped track the health status of Americans, their access to health care, and the nation's progress toward achieving health goals.

Contact us

Email nhis@cdc.gov with any questions about the National Health Interview Survey.

Related NHIS surveys

  • NHIS–Teen
  • 2014 Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS

New: 2025 National Health Interview Survey Public-use Files

For Everyone
Sept. 30, 2026

What to know

NCHS releases the 2025 NHIS public-use files.

Summary

A data story from the National Center for Health Statistics

Author: Danielle Taylor

Get the data story

The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) has released the 2025 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) public-use files. These files provide the most current data on chronic conditions, chronic pain, healthcare access, and disability, based on information collected from more than 25,000 households. They include survey questions, responses, and nonidentifying information about respondents to protect privacy.

What is NHIS?

NHIS is an annual survey that collects information from adults and children on a variety of health topics. It helps doctors, journalists, researchers, and policymakers track health trends and guide medical advice and policy.

NHIS data can answer questions like—

  • Where do most people get their health insurance?
  • How do people use the Internet to get medical information?
  • Are cancer screenings common?
  • In what ways do people manage pain?

What's new in the 2025 survey

The 2025 survey included questions about social connection and isolation, menopausal health, and caregiving.

The survey description provides details on how NHIS topics were selected. You can explore the files to learn how the survey was developed, request access to restricted detailed data, and run your own analyses.

Available products and tools

We also want to make it easy for you to incorporate the most recent national estimates in your communications. Updated 2025 estimates are available in the NCHS Data Query System (DQS). Our User Guide provides instructions on how to filter DQS by data source to help you find NHIS estimates.

Give feedback and get updates

NCHS is seeking feedback on a planned redesign for the 2028 survey to modernize data collection and make participation easier. This is an important opportunity for people to have a say in the future of the nation's oldest and largest household health survey. Written comments must be received on or before October 20, 2026.

Join the NHIS listserv to get news about upcoming reports and data releases. For questions about NHIS or the 2025 files, contact staff from the NCHS Division of Health Interview Statistics at nhislist@cdc.gov.

2028 NHIS Questionnaire Redesign

For Everyone
Aug. 21, 2026

What to know

  • The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) is proposing updates to the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS).
  • NCHS is redesigning NHIS to modernize its data collection process.
  • The redesign is in response to rising costs, growing difficulty in reaching households, and the need for a more flexible and efficient survey.

Overview

CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) has proposed a redesign of the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). Since 1957, NHIS has collected and analyzed health data to monitor the health of people across the country.

The proposed NHIS redesign includes—

  • Revisions to the adult and child questionnaires
  • Use of a sequential mixed-mode data collection design with self-response options

Changes to the questionnaires are intended to improve the measurement of contemporary health topics and reduce respondent burden through shorter and less complex instruments.

The redesign reflects the ongoing need to maintain a gold-standard national health survey while adapting to increasing data collection costs and respondent preferences by incorporating lower-cost, self-administered data collection modes.

NHIS was previously redesigned in 1997 and 2019.

Proposed content

Review the draft questionnaires and a brief description of the redesign (in the Federal Register) to learn more—

  • Adult Questionnaire
  • Child Questionnaire
  • Federal Register Notice

Public comment

NCHS invites public comment on all areas of the proposed redesign. Comments are especially welcome regarding—

  • Structure, length, and clarity of the revised questionnaire
  • Shift to a sequential mixed mode design
  • Proposed addition or removal of content
  • How these changes may affect data quality, usability, and trends over time

Commenters who suggest questionnaire additions are encouraged to identify the minimum question sets to meet identified data needs.

NCHS is also interested in comments on the practical utility of child-level data collection that is largely limited to domains for which all-person population estimates are desired (i.e., population estimates that have historically relied on data from both the adult and child-focused interviews).

Questions?

Email healthsurveys@cdc.gov with any questions about the 2028 redesign.

Comment submission

Written comments must be received on or before October 20, 2026.

You may submit comments, identified by Docket No. CDC-2026-1387 by any of the following methods:

  • Federal eRulemaking Portal:
    • Go to the Federal Register Notice
    • Click on the blue "Comment" button at the top to submit comments
  • Mail: Jeffrey M. Zirger, Information Collection Review Office, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1600 Clifton Road, N.E., MS-D74, Atlanta, Georgia 30329

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Health Interview Survey
Organization/publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCHS)
Description: The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of the U.S. population by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics for children and adults. Conducted by CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, it is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey, collecting data since 1957 from about 27,000 adults each year through confidential, face-to-face interviews.
URL: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# National Health Interview Survey (NHIS): Dataset Report

*Researched October 2026. Sources are official CDC/NCHS and Census Bureau pages, NCHS methods documents, OMB filings, IPUMS, and recent policy coverage.*

---

## 1. Fact-check of your description

Your description is mostly accurate. It closely follows the wording on CDC's current "About NHIS" page, but a few points need qualifying.

| Your claim | Verdict | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Publisher: CDC / NCHS | ✅ Correct | NCHS, part of CDC within HHS, runs the survey. The U.S. Census Bureau collects the data under contract. Within NCHS, the **Division of Health Interview Statistics** is responsible. |
| Monitors health of U.S. children and adults across many topics | ✅ Correct | Matches CDC wording. |
| "Nation's largest and oldest national health survey" | ⚠️ CDC's own claim, but needs context | CDC uses this phrase. Elsewhere it uses "largest and oldest *household* health survey." The "largest" claim is best read as applying to in-person household health surveys. CDC's phone-based BRFSS interviews far more people each year. |
| Collecting data since 1957 | ✅ Correct, with a nuance | Official data collection began the first week of July 1957, under the National Health Survey Act signed July 3, 1956. Digital microdata files only go back to **1963**. |
| "About 27,000 adults each year" | ⚠️ Outdated and varies | This is CDC's current boilerplate, but actual counts change a lot by year: **32,629** adults and 8,360 children in 2024, and **24,215** adults and 6,049 children in 2025. |
| "Confidential, face-to-face interviews" | ⚠️ Partly true | Interviews are confidential and usually start in person. But in 2024, 53.2% of adult interviews were done at least partly by phone, and in 2025 it was 53.1%. NCHS is also now testing paper and online questionnaires. |
| URL https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html | ✅ Live | |

---

## 2. Publisher and how it's organized

- **Sponsor/owner:** National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), CDC, HHS. NCHS is the nation's principal health statistical agency, one of the official federal statistical agencies.
- **Data collection:** The U.S. Census Bureau hires and trains the field representatives, who follow NCHS procedures. The Bureau does this work under Title 13, U.S.C. §8(b). Census has been NCHS's field partner since the survey began.
- **Contacts:** nhis@cdc.gov (general questions), nhislist@cdc.gov (data users), healthsurveys@cdc.gov (the 2028 redesign), nhis@census.gov (people selected to take part). There is also an NHIS listserv.
- **OMB clearance:** OMB No. 0920-0214, currently set to expire 12/31/2026. An extension for 2027 was out for public comment in August–October 2026.

## 3. Legal authority and confidentiality

- **Authority to collect:** Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 242k), the law that created NCHS. It descends from the **National Health Survey Act of 1956** (P.L. 84-652). That act authorized "continuing surveys and special studies" of illness and disability. It also told the Public Health Service to "develop and test new or improved methods" for collecting the data.
- **Confidentiality protections:**
  - PHS Act §308(d) (42 U.S.C. 242m(d)): data may be used only for the purposes described to respondents.
  - CIPSEA 2018 (44 U.S.C. 3561–3583), enacted as part of the Evidence Act. Willfully disclosing identifiable information can bring up to 5 years in prison, a $250,000 fine, or both.
  - Privacy Act of 1974.
  - Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act.
- **User terms:** The public-use files come with binding conditions. Data may be used only for statistical reporting and analysis, and users may make no attempt to identify anyone.

## 4. History

- **1956:** Congress passes the National Health Survey Act with bipartisan support, following earlier committee recommendations. President Eisenhower signs it July 3, 1956.
- **1957:** A pretest of 1,200 households in Charlotte, NC, followed by a nationwide dry run in May–June. Official data collection begins July 1957. The first design sampled 372 primary sampling units and about 36,000 households (around 115,000 people) a year.
- **1960 onward:** The household sample is redesigned after each decennial census (1985, 1995, 2006, 2016 designs). The post-1980-census redesign made more geographic detail possible, allowed linkage to administrative records, and let NHIS serve as a sampling frame for other surveys.
- **1982:** The questionnaire is split into a core section plus topical supplements.
- **1997:** Major questionnaire redesign to reduce respondent burden, introducing family, sample adult, and sample child modules. Computer-assisted interviewing (CAPI) is used.
- **2016:** New sample design. About 70% of the sample is allocated in proportion to state population. The other ~30% can be reallocated, for example to oversample groups or small states, which allows three-year estimates for all states.
- **2019:** Questionnaire redesign. The family module is dropped, leaving one randomly chosen adult and one randomly chosen child per household. Content is now annual core plus rotating, sponsored, and emerging topics. Estimates from 2019 on are not directly comparable to 1997–2018.
- **2020:** COVID-19 disrupted in-person fieldwork, and telephone interviewing expanded.
- **2025:**
  - Data collection stopped from **October 1 to November 16, 2025** because of the lapse in appropriations.
  - Response rates were also hurt by trouble hiring and keeping field staff, and by a federal travel moratorium.
  - NHIS-Teen was not fielded.
  - New topics included social connection and isolation, menopausal health, and caregiving.
  - The 2025 public-use files came out September 30, 2026.
- **2028 (proposed):** A third major redesign. Questionnaires would be shorter and less complex, and data would be collected through a **sequential mixed-mode design with self-response (web/paper) options**. CDC cites rising costs and growing difficulty reaching households. Comments were due by October 19–20, 2026 (Docket CDC-2026-1387). NCHS is also asking whether child-level data collection is worth keeping beyond the topics needed for whole-population estimates.

## 5. Methods (for data scientists)

- **Population covered:** Civilian, noninstitutionalized people in the 50 states and DC. Excluded: active-duty military, civilians living on military bases, and people in long-term care, prisons, and psychiatric hospitals.
- **Design:** Stratified, multistage probability sample, collected continuously through the year. Each month and quarter is nationally representative. The design targets national, regional, and metro/nonmetro estimates within regions. It is **not designed for precise annual estimates in every state**, and state identifiers are only available in restricted files.
- **Who answers:**
  - A household roster for everyone in the household.
  - One sample adult, self-reporting unless a proxy is needed.
  - One sample child (age 17 or under), reported by a knowledgeable adult.
- **Response rates (AAPOR RR2):**
  - 2023: sample adult 47.0%.
  - 2024: sample adult 47.9%, sample child 45.8%, household 49.7%.
  - 2025: weighted sample adult 41.3%, sample child 42.0%. Weighted rates are now reported, with retroactive figures back to 2019.
  - The decline matters for assessing nonresponse bias.
- **Analysis requirements:** Use the survey weights and design variables (strata/PSU) for variance estimation. NCHS publishes a **PRICSSA** checklist for reporting complex-survey analyses. A public-use **paradata file** describes the data collection process.
- **Burden:** About 49 minutes per sample adult interview. The 2025 annual estimate was about 37,900 burden hours in total.

## 6. Topics covered

Chronic conditions and illness; injuries and chronic pain; health behaviors (tobacco, alcohol, physical activity); functioning and disability; access to and use of health care; **health insurance coverage**; preventive services and screenings; mental health; plus rotating and sponsored modules. Answers can be broken down by demographics, region, metro status, income/poverty, employment, and more.

## 7. Ways to access the data

| Access tier | What's available |
|---|---|
| **Public-use files** | Annual microdata, questionnaires, codebooks, and survey descriptions on the NCHS site and FTP server (ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/). Downloadable in several formats, with all identifying information removed. |
| **Early Release Program** | Quarterly and semiannual estimates on key indicators, especially insurance coverage, published before the annual files. |
| **Interactive tools** | NCHS Data Query System (DQS) and NHIS interactive summary health statistics for adults and children. |
| **Restricted data** | Through the NCHS Research Data Center, for a fee. Applications go through the Standard Application Process at researchdatagov.org. Includes geography such as state and county. |
| **Linked data** | NHIS linked to the National Death Index. Restricted files cover 1986–2021 survey years with deaths through 12/31/2022; public-use mortality files cover 1986–2018, with some values replaced by synthetic ones to protect privacy. Restricted links also exist to CMS Medicare and Medicaid, HUD housing assistance, and VA records. |
| **IPUMS Health Surveys: NHIS** (Univ. of Minnesota) | Free, harmonized microdata from 1963 to the present, with over 17,000 consistently coded variables and integrated mortality links. Versions have DOIs (current: 10.18128/D070.V8.1). This is the best route for long-term trend work. |
| **MEPS** | AHRQ's Medical Expenditure Panel Survey draws its sample from NHIS respondents, so the two can be linked. |

Related products include the **2014 Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS** and **NHIS-Teen**, a self-response follow-up of adolescents that was not fielded in 2025 and might be in 2026.

## 8. Typical users

- **Federal agencies:** HHS, CDC programs, CMS, ASPE, AHRQ, Census, and CBO, for tracking insurance coverage and assessing policy changes such as the ACA. Also used for Healthy People objectives and *Health, United States*.
- **Academic researchers:** epidemiology, health economics, demography, disparities research, and mortality studies using the linked files. IPUMS keeps a large bibliography of this work.
- **State and local health departments and think tanks:** e.g., SHADAC, KFF, Urban Institute, Commonwealth Fund.
- **Journalists, clinicians, advocates, and the public:** CDC describes NHIS as helping "doctors, journalists, researchers, and policymakers track health trends."

## 9. Benefits to the public

- Official national estimates of uninsurance, chronic disease, disability, and access to care, with almost 70 years of continuity.
- Large enough samples to compare subgroups by race/ethnicity, income, age, and other characteristics, which supports equity analysis.
- Evidence for evaluating federal health programs and tracking national health goals.
- Infrastructure for other surveys: it is MEPS's sampling frame, and its address lists and methods support other federal surveys.
- Links to death and administrative records make it possible to study long-term outcomes without new data collection.
- It is free and openly documented, which helps transparency and lets others reproduce results.

## 10. Current risks (for policy advocates and preservationists)

- **Staffing:** On October 10, 2025, reduction-in-force notices hit NCHS, more than 100 staff or nearly 25% of its workforce, mostly support, methods, IT security, and communications roles. Many notices were rescinded in November 2025 as part of the deal to reopen the government (AJPH, 2026).
- **Funding:**
  - NCHS received $187.4M in FY2026.
  - The President's FY2027 request was $175M; the House bill kept $187.4M.
  - The Friends of NCHS coalition asked for $220M, citing a 24% loss in purchasing power since FY2010.
- **Data quality pressures:** Response rates are falling, field staff are hard to keep, there is a gap in 2025 data collection, and the 2025 sample is smaller.
- **Breaks in trends:** The 2019 redesign already broke comparability. The 2028 mixed-mode redesign will likely cause another break from mode effects and content changes, and could cut child data. The open comment docket is the main way for the public to have a say.

## 11. Preservation notes (for data librarians)

- **Main stores:** the NCHS FTP server (data, documentation, questionnaires, and field manuals back through decades), the archive.cdc.gov snapshot of the old NHIS site (including 1997 redesign material), and CDC Stacks for publications such as *Vital and Health Statistics* Series 10 and the Series 2 methods reports.
- **Independent copies:** IPUMS NHIS (versioned with DOIs, 1963 onward). ICPSR also holds historical NHIS releases.
- **Recommended to capture:** annual public-use files plus survey descriptions, codebooks, questionnaires, field representative manuals, and PRICSSA checklists; the paradata files; the linked mortality public-use files; the 2028 redesign drafts and Federal Register notices; and OMB package documents from reginfo.gov or omb.report.
- **Citation:** cite NCHS, National Health Interview Survey, [year], public-use data file and documentation, plus the IPUMS DOI if you use harmonized data.

- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.

- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.

# NHIS Risk Assessment

*Assessed October 2026. NHIS = National Health Interview Survey, run by CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS).*

**Bottom line:** The survey is not close to ending. Its legal basis is solid and its funding is roughly flat. The real risks are a thinner survey, delays, policy-driven content removal, a possible move out of CDC, and the 2028 redesign. Back up the files and documentation now, especially from before 2028.

**A note on the staffing tracker:** I checked usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com. It counts job postings, not actual staff, and it stopped updating on December 31, 2025. I couldn't pull NCHS-specific figures from it, so the staffing numbers below come from the American Statistical Association (ASA) and AJPH.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for no known issue**
- The NCHS FTP server still has the public-use files, documentation and questionnaires going back decades. The 2024 files (posted June 30, 2025) are intact, and NCHS published checksums for them (Checksum-filelist.pdf), so copies can be verified.
- The University of Minnesota's IPUMS keeps an independent, versioned copy of harmonized microdata from 1963 on.
- I found no reports of NHIS data files being removed or edited.

**Evidence for moderate risk**
- In January–February 2025, CDC took down many web pages to comply with Executive Order 14168 (the "gender ideology" order). Researchers reported that some restored CDC datasets and codebooks had demographic variables removed. Those reports were about CDC generally, not NHIS.
- In September 2025, HHS ordered more CDC pages on sexual and gender identity and health equity removed (CNBC).
- I could not confirm whether the gender identity variables in the 2022–2024 NHIS files are still present. That is worth checking against archived copies.

**Rating: No Known Issue.** Nothing shows NHIS files were removed or changed. The CDC-wide takedowns are a reason to verify the files against the published checksums and IPUMS copies.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for no known issue**
- The OMB approval to collect data (No. 0920-0214, reference 202601-0920-011) is active through December 31, 2026.
- A renewal covering 2027–2029 was published on time in the Federal Register (91 FR 53869, August 20, 2026).
- The 2025 data were released, and the 2025 early insurance estimates came out May 28, 2026, about the usual time.

**Evidence for moderate risk**
- The 2025 public-use files came out September 30, 2026. The usual release is late June (the 2024 files posted June 30, 2025), so this was about three months late.
- Data collection stopped from October 1 to mid-November 2025 during the shutdown. The 2025 sample was smaller: 24,215 adults, versus 32,629 in 2024.
- The January–June 2025 early estimates came out January 30, 2026. The equivalent 2024 report came out December 6, 2024.
- NHIS-Teen, a follow-up survey of adolescents, was not run in 2025.

**Evidence for high risk:** none. Skipping NHIS-Teen is a skipped component, not the main survey.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** Publication and collection were delayed, but the approval is current and renewal is under way.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for high risk**
- **Less frequent releases:** starting in 2026, the early estimates moved from quarterly to twice a year (SHADAC; NHIS website).
- **Less detail:** the gender identity questions and their write-in follow-up were dropped in 2025 (OMB change request of March 20, 2025; KFF; SHADAC).
- **Less timely:** the 2025 files were three months late, and the 2025 data have a six-week gap and a smaller sample.
- Weighted response rates fell to 41.3% for adults and 42.0% for children in 2025, down from 47.9% and 45.8% in 2024. NCHS blamed trouble hiring field staff and a federal travel moratorium.
- NHIS-Teen was skipped in 2025.

**Evidence for further risk ahead**
- The 2028 redesign would shorten the questionnaires and switch to web and paper first, with in-person follow-up. Changing how people respond will likely break trend comparisons.
- The disability research group HSRI found that the draft drops detailed disability questions, including age of onset and two questions sponsored by HHS's Administration for Community Living (ACL).
- NCHS is openly asking whether child-level data are worth collecting.

**Rating: High Risk.** Frequency, detail and timeliness have all already declined.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for no known issue**
- Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 242k) explicitly directs NCHS to collect statistics on "the extent and nature of illness and disability" in the U.S. population. This goes back to the National Health Survey Act of 1956.
- NHIS is a leading source for *Health, United States*, a report Congress requires.
- CDC calls it "the single most important source of statistics" for tracking HHS health goals (Healthy People 2030).
- AHRQ's Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) draws its sample from NHIS respondents, so MEPS depends on it.
- No other survey can fully replace it. BRFSS (phone, state-based), the Census Bureau's ACS and CPS (narrower health content) and NHANES (much smaller sample) each cover only part of what NHIS does.

**Evidence for moderate risk**
- The law names the subject but not specific questions or how often to collect, so NCHS has wide latitude to reshape content, as the 2028 proposal shows.
- Other surveys can substitute for some topics, such as insurance coverage via the ACS.

**Rating: No Known Issue.** The authorization is explicit, federal programs depend on it, and nothing fully substitutes for it.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for moderate risk**
- ASA's 2026 midyear report puts NCHS staff losses at about 14–20% from the end of FY2024 to mid-FY2026.
- On October 10, 2025, more than 100 NCHS staff (nearly 25%) received layoff notices. Many were rescinded in November under the deal that reopened the government (AJPH, 2026). Before that, an estimated 85–90 notices were still in effect, mostly in IT and research methods, which affects NCHS's ability to publish data and improve methods.
- **Leadership:** CDC's NCHS director page has listed the post as "Vacant" since January 6, 2026. NCHS advertised the job July 16, 2026. Of 19 branch chiefs, 9 are acting.
- **Budget:** FY2026 was $187.4M, flat. The FY2027 request is $175M, a 6.6% cut, and the House bill keeps $187.4M. Friends of NCHS, a coalition of supporting organizations, says purchasing power has fallen 24% since FY2010.
- **Structure:** the FY2026 and FY2027 budget requests propose moving NCHS out of CDC into a new HHS "Office of Strategy" with ASPE and AHRQ. That office as a whole would be cut 20.5%.
- The Census Bureau, which does the interviewing, is struggling to hire and keep field staff and also has no confirmed director.

**Evidence for high risk:** staff losses are under 40%, the budget cut is under 20%, and I found no evidence the director was forced out. The vacancy is real but its cause is unclear.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.**

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for high risk**
- NCHS asked OMB to change the 2025 questionnaire specifically to comply with Executive Order 14168, removing the gender identity questions (change request of March 20, 2025). NCHS confirmed this to NPR. This is an information collection change driven by a Presidential action.
- CDC-wide page removals in 2025 followed the same order.

**Evidence for moderate risk**
- The 2028 redesign is pending (Docket CDC-2026-1387; comments due October 19–20, 2026). It would shorten the questionnaires, change how people respond, may cut child data, and drops disability questions.
- The proposed move of NCHS into the HHS Office of Strategy is still pending.

**Rating: High Risk.** A Presidential order directly changed what the survey collects.

---

## Summary of risk levels
- Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue**
- Future Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**
- Data Quality: **High Risk**
- Statutory Context: **No Known Issue**
- Staffing and Funding: **Moderate Risk**
- Policy: **High Risk**
